HB152 (2025) exempts these items from the state portion of sales/use tax only, from Sep. 1, 2025 through Aug. 31, 2028. Rafferty sponsored it and Marques is not on the bill's list; the House passed it unanimously. But Marques's launch statement was that he 'worked in the Alabama Legislature to eliminate the state tax on diapers and baby supplies.' The paraphrase 'Eliminated…' overstates what he claimed, so 'overstates his role' is weak. The fair basis for 'partly' is that the exemption is temporary and covers state tax only.
results.fix: Claim: Said he 'worked in the Alabama Legislature to eliminate the state tax on diapers and baby supplies.' Record: HB152 (sponsor Rep. Neil Rafferty, D; passed House unanimously) removes only the state portion of sales/use tax, and only from Sep. 1, 2025 to Aug. 31, 2028. Local taxes still apply unless local governments opt in. Calling the tax 'eliminated' omits that the exemption is temporary and state-only. Verdict: partly.

results.finding: Figures's campaign statement is confirmed: 'voting for a 67 percent tax increase on gas and diesel.' Marques's 2019 Rebuild Alabama vote is documented. But the item's own record says the 67% figure was never checked, and no source I could reach explains it. A 'partly' verdict with no checked basis should not move the score. Unchecked background from the act's terms: it raises gas from 18¢ to 28¢ (≈56%) and diesel from 19¢ to 29¢ (≈53%), then indexes up to 1¢ every two years from 2023. If gas has reached ≈30¢, that is ≈67% for gasoline, so the claim may be closer to accurate than 'partly'.
results.fix: Rate this claim only after checking the ALDOT/Department of Revenue fuel-tax schedule. Until then, list it unrated with the record: 'Marques voted for the 2019 Rebuild Alabama Act (phased 10¢ increase from 18¢ gas / 19¢ diesel, plus inflation indexing from 2023); the 67% figure has not been independently checked.'

The promise is documented. Reflector: he said in 2014 he 'would only serve 10 years.' Wikipedia: he said no more than five terms and acknowledged it in March 2023 ('own that'). He ran for a sixth term in 2024 and is the 2026 nominee. But the record misattributes the U.S. Term Limits accusation: it was about refusing to cosponsor a term-limits amendment (2021), not the 10-year promise, and his campaign called that 'fake news.' He said he 'prayed for God to give me clarity'; the Reflector says he 'claimed that God gave him clarity.' A promise is better scored as a broken promise (saydo) than a 'false' claim, and the two items double-count.
results.fix: Record: During his 2014 campaign he said he would serve no more than five terms (10 years); he acknowledged the statement in March 2023. He ran for a sixth term in 2024 and is the 2026 nominee for a seventh, saying he had prayed for clarity from God. He argues his signed U.S. Term Limits pledge covered only sponsoring term-limits legislation. (Separately, U.S. Term Limits accused him in 2021 of breaking that pledge by not cosponsoring its amendment.) Consider scoring this only as the saydo item to avoid double-counting.
